notes.meaning: When the tribes receive their inheritance in the land, God commands that a sacred section be set apart for Him before anyone else receives property. This holy portion is measured out first to show that worship and God's presence are the most important part of national life. Setting it aside acts like a first-fruits gift that dedicates the whole land to the Lord.

differ.view: Expect a literal measurement and division of land around a future earthly temple during the millennium.
Understands this land grant spiritually as a picture of Christ's church, noting that the measurements would be larger than the historic land of Canaan.

notes.meaning: A specific square area inside the holy district is set aside for the temple building and its courts. An open border of empty land surrounds the sanctuary on every side. This open space keeps ordinary homes and daily business from crowding against the holy house of God.

A large territory within the sacred district is reserved for the priests who draw near to serve the Lord, with the Most Holy Place situated in its center. The priests build their homes in this area so they can live right next to the sanctuary. Living close to their place of work allows them to carry out their duties faithfully without being scattered across the country.

Another large strip of land right beside the priests' section belongs to the Levites, who assist with temple duties. In earlier times under Moses, the Levites were scattered across Israel without a single unified territory. Here they are given their own dedicated district to live in and manage together.

A section of land next to the holy district is designated for the capital city. Unlike the tribal territories, this city is open to people from every tribe in Israel rather than belonging to just one. It provides a common dwelling and gathering place for the whole nation.

The prince is granted land on both the east and west sides of the sacred area and the city, stretching out toward the country's outer borders. Placing his property directly beside the sacred portion shows his close relationship with God's house and his duty to defend it. Having his own large territory ensures he has sufficient resources to maintain his position.

This land provides the ruler with a permanent and secure estate in Israel. In past generations, selfish rulers often used heavy taxes and seized family properties to build their own wealth. With a generous personal inheritance, future rulers will no longer oppress the people or take away their tribal lands.

God commands the rulers of Israel to halt their violent ways, stop stealing, and start doing what is right and just. They are strictly ordered to end the practice of driving poor families off their rightful land. Those who lead God's people must practice genuine justice instead of abusing their power.

God establishes honest, uniform standards for weights and measures across the nation. The ephah for dry grain and the bath for liquid wine and oil are fixed to the same standard size, while the weight of the silver shekel and mina is clearly settled. God insists on complete honesty in the marketplace because cheating a neighbor ruins the integrity of true worship.

God defines the regular contributions the people must bring from their harvest and herds: a sixtieth of their grain, a hundredth of their olive oil, and one healthy sheep from every two hundred. These gifts supply the sacrifices needed to make atonement, which means restoring peace and covering sin between God and His people. Bringing animals from the richest pastures shows that the Lord deserves the very best of what He provides.

Every person in Israel must bring these appointed contributions to the prince. The prince then uses these gifts to provide the official sacrifices for the Sabbath days, the monthly new moons, and all the annual festivals. This arrangement makes sure that public worship is maintained steadily and that the altar is never left without offerings.

The new year opens on the first day of the first month with a special cleansing ceremony not found in the earlier law of Moses. A young bull without defect is sacrificed, and the priest puts its blood on the temple doorposts, the corners of the altar, and the inner court gates. This ritual removes the uncleanness caused by human weakness so the sanctuary enters the new year pure before God.

On the seventh day of that same opening month, another purification offering is made for anyone who has sinned through ignorance, carelessness, or human weakness. This ceremony cleanses the temple from the unintentional faults of priests, Levites, and common people alike. It demonstrates God's willingness to make full provision for people when they go astray without malice.

Two weeks into the first month, Israel gathers to observe the Passover and eat unleavened bread for seven days. This festival celebrates God freeing His people from slavery in Egypt and saving them from judgment. It reminds believers to live clean lives and put away old sinful ways like bread made without yeast.

On the opening day of Passover, the prince must present a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people. Because the ruler is required to offer a sacrifice for his own personal faults, he is a mortal human leader rather than the sinless Messiah. Even the highest earthly authority must acknowledge his own shortcomings before the Lord.

differ.view: Understands the prince providing the offerings as a symbol of Christ, who made atonement for His people through His own sacrifice.
Believes the prince is a human ruler, such as David, because he needs a sin offering for his own guilt, which could never apply to Jesus.

notes.meaning: During each of the seven feast days, the prince provides seven bulls, seven rams, and a male goat, along with generous measures of flour and olive oil. These daily offerings are much larger and richer than the sacrifices Moses originally prescribed. Such large gifts reflect the great abundance and joyful dedication of God's renewed people.

Six months later, during the autumn Feast of Tabernacles, the prince provides the exact same daily sacrifices of animals, grain, and oil for seven days. Keeping this full schedule of offerings shows that grateful praise and worship remain central throughout every season. It highlights the constant need for God's forgiving mercy all through the year.
